message:
QUESTION:
How much did the average-speed cameras reduce injury collisions at the 10 sites, and what would a city-wide rollout achieve?

DATA:
Average-speed cameras at 10 sites, installed January 2023. The 10 sites were chosen because they had the highest numbers of injury collisions in the city in 2020-2022.

| | 2020-2022 (3 years before) | 2023-2025 (3 years after) |
| Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites | 156 | 102 |
| Injury collisions on all other city roads | 3,600 | 3,240 |

Traffic: a bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Traffic counts at the 10 sites fell by an average of 15% between the two periods. Traffic on other city roads was broadly unchanged.

Speed surveys at the camera sites (speed limit 30 mph): mean speed 34 mph before installation, 31 mph after.

The 10 sites are all urban arterial roads. The city has about 900 km of roads, of which the camera sites cover about 12 km. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [method] Ignores regression to the mean. The sites were selected because their 2020-2022 counts were the highest, so that period is likely inflated by chance, and counts would be expected to fall even without cameras. CORRECTION: The before period overstates the true underlying rate. An RTM adjustment (e.g. an empirical-Bayes estimate using longer histories or comparable sites) is needed, and the 27% figure is an upper bound.
F2. [omission] Ignores the 15% fall in traffic at the sites after the bypass opened, which would reduce collisions on its own. CORRECTION: Expected without cameras, allowing for trend and traffic: 52 × 0.90 × 0.85 = 39.8 a year, so about 6 prevented a year (roughly a 15% relative reduction), before any RTM adjustment.
F3. [misreport] The surveys show mean speed fell from 34 to 31 mph, still above the 30 mph limit. CORRECTION: A 3 mph fall in mean speed; speeds remain slightly above the limit.
F4. [inference] Generalises from 12 km of the highest-collision arterial roads to 900 km of mostly low-collision residential streets, with a selection-inflated effect estimate. CORRECTION: No city-wide estimate is supported. The effect on typical roads, which have low counts, would be much smaller in absolute terms and is unknown in relative terms.

EXTENSIONS:
- Request each site's collision counts for earlier years (e.g. 2015-2019) to estimate the regression-to-the-mean component directly.
- Split the 10 sites into the 6 affected by the bypass and the 4 not affected; the 4 unaffected sites give a cleaner (if small) estimate of the camera effect.
- Look at severity (killed or seriously injured vs slight), since speed reductions are expected to reduce severity more than frequency; even a modest 3 mph fall in mean speed may matter there.

FINAL VERSION:
# Average-Speed Cameras: Three-Year Evaluation (Revised)

## Summary

Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites fell by 35%, from 156 to 102. After allowing for the city-wide trend, the fall is about 27%. That figure overstates what the cameras achieved, for two reasons:

- **The sites were picked for their unusually high 2020-2022 counts.** Some of the later fall would have happened anyway (regression to the mean).
- **A bypass opened in March 2023 and cut traffic at the sites by 15%.** Traffic on the comparison roads did not change.

Allowing for the traffic fall alone brings the estimated camera effect down to roughly 15%. That estimate is statistically uncertain and is still inflated by regression to the mean. The cameras probably helped. Mean speeds fell from 34 to 31 mph. But the data cannot tell us by how much.

The results do not support a forecast for a city-wide rollout. In particular, the draft's figure of about 290 collisions prevented a year should not be used.

## Background

Average-speed cameras were installed at 10 sites in January 2023. This note compares injury collisions over three full years before (2020-2022) and three full years after (2023-2025). It looks at the 10 sites and at all other city roads.

All 10 sites are urban arterial roads. Together they cover about 12 km of the city's 900 km network, about 1.3% of its length. They are much more collision-dense than the rest of the network:

- **Camera sites (before):** about 4.3 injury collisions per km per year (52 a year over 12 km).
- **All other roads:** about 1.35 per km per year (1,200 a year over 888 km).

## Raw change

| | 2020-2022 | 2023-2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Camera sites | 156 (52/yr) | 102 (34/yr) | −35% |
| All other roads | 3,600 (1,200/yr) | 3,240 (1,080/yr) | −10% |

## Allowing for the background trend

The ratio of after to before at the sites is 0.654. On other roads it is 0.900. Dividing one by the other gives 0.727, a relative reduction of about 27%.

Put another way, the 10% background fall would have taken the sites from 52 to an expected 46.8 collisions a year. The observed figure is 34, a gap of about 13 a year.

This 27% is an upper-end estimate. Three problems mean the true camera effect is smaller, and less certain, than it suggests.

### 1. Regression to the mean

The sites were chosen because they had the city's highest injury-collision counts in 2020-2022. A site's count in any period reflects its underlying risk plus random variation. Sites picked for high counts will tend to have had bad luck in that period. Their counts would be expected to fall afterwards even if nothing changed.

The 2020-2022 period is therefore not a fair baseline. It is biased upwards, and part of the 35% fall is an artefact of how the sites were chosen. We cannot size this bias from the data here. Studies of speed-camera schemes have often found it to be a substantial share of the apparent effect.

To estimate it, we would need either:

- collision counts at the sites for earlier years (for example 2015-2019), or
- an empirical Bayes analysis using similar arterial roads without cameras.

### 2. The bypass reduced traffic at the sites

The bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Average traffic at the sites fell by 15%. Traffic on the comparison roads was broadly unchanged. So the comparison roads do not account for this.

Assume, roughly, that collisions scale with traffic volume. Then the expected count without cameras is about 46.8 × 0.85 ≈ 39.8 a year, against 34 observed. That implies a camera effect of about 6 collisions a year, or roughly 15% (0.727 / 0.85 ≈ 0.855).

The relationship between traffic and collisions is not exactly proportional, so this is approximate. A site-by-site comparison would help: the 6 bypass-affected sites against the 4 unaffected ones.

### 3. Small numbers

The counts at the sites are small, so random variation matters. Treating the counts as Poisson gives approximate 95% intervals:

- **Unadjusted ratio of 0.727:** about 0.56 to 0.94, a reduction somewhere between 6% and 44%.
- **Traffic-adjusted ratio of about 0.855:** roughly 0.66 to 1.1. This is consistent with anything from a sizeable reduction to no effect.

Both intervals exist before any allowance for regression to the mean.

## Speeds

Speed surveys at the sites show mean speeds falling from 34 mph to 31 mph. That is a 3 mph reduction, which still leaves the mean slightly above the 30 mph limit.

A fall of this size is consistent with some real reduction in collision risk and severity. It is the clearest direct evidence that the cameras changed driver behaviour. However, the bypass may also have changed the traffic mix and speeds at the affected sites, so not all of the speed change can be credited to the cameras.

## City-wide rollout

The evaluation does not support an estimate of what a city-wide rollout would achieve. Applying a 27% reduction to all 1,080 collisions a year on other roads is not valid, for three reasons:

- **The 27% is itself overstated**, because of regression to the mean and the bypass.
- **It was measured on 12 km of high-collision arterial roads.** Most of the remaining 888 km is residential streets with low collision counts and different traffic conditions. Average-speed cameras are designed for corridors and are rarely suited to residential streets. There is no basis for assuming the same percentage effect there.
- **The benefit per camera falls steeply as you move to lower-risk roads.** Low collision counts mean few collisions to prevent per km, against similar installation and running costs.

Any extension should be framed as targeted deployment on other high-risk arterial corridors, not as a city-wide programme.

## Recommendations

1. **Do not fund a city-wide programme on the basis of this evaluation.**
2. **Re-analyse the existing sites before deciding on extension.** Specifically:
   - obtain pre-2020 collision data for the 10 sites, or carry out an empirical Bayes analysis, to estimate regression to the mean;
   - analyse the 6 bypass-affected and 4 unaffected sites separately;
   - use comparison sites of the same road type (arterials), not all other roads;
   - examine collision severity as well as counts.
3. **If the corrected effect remains worthwhile, pilot cameras on a small number of further high-risk arterial corridors.** Design the pilot so it can be evaluated properly, for example with comparable control corridors and baselines that are not the same years used for site selection.
4. **Continue annual monitoring** of collisions and speeds at the original 10 sites.

## Costs and publication

Average-speed camera systems carry installation, maintenance and enforcement costs. A business case for any extension should set these against a corrected estimate of the collisions prevented, valued by severity. The evaluation, including its limitations, should be published so residents can see the results.

---

## Main changes from the draft

- **Speed figure corrected.** The data show the mean falling to 31 mph, not 26 mph. That is still above the 30 mph limit, not "well below" it.
- **Site selection.** The draft called the 2020-2022 baseline "fair". Because the sites were chosen for their high counts in that period, the baseline is biased upwards (regression to the mean).
- **Bypass added.** The draft ignored the bypass, which cut traffic at the sites by 15% but not on the comparison roads. Adjusting for it roughly halves the estimated effect, to about 15%.
- **Uncertainty quantified.** I added approximate statistical intervals. After the traffic adjustment, they do not rule out no effect.
- **City-wide claim removed.** The draft applied a 27% cut to the whole network, giving about 290 collisions a year. I removed this, because the result comes from 12 km of high-risk arterials and most of the network is low-collision residential streets.
- **Recommendation changed.** It now calls for a corrected analysis and targeted, well-evaluated extension instead of city-wide funding.
- **Arithmetic retained.** The draft's arithmetic (35%, 10%, 0.727, 46.8 vs 34) was correct and is kept.
